Dynamic, Sound and Colour Marks in China: What the New Law Now Allows

The revised Trademark Law, effective 1 January 2027, addresses non-conventional signs expressly: Article 14 adds dynamic marks, and Article 18 sets out a functionality-based exclusion for colour, sound and dynamic signs. The filing details come from draft guidelines and may still change.

What Changes on 1 January 2027

The Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) was adopted on 26 June 2026 and takes effect on 1 January 2027. It has nine chapters and 87 articles. Among its most visible changes is Article 14, which adds dynamic signs to the types of sign that may be registered, and Article 18, which sets out a functionality-based exclusion for colour, sound and dynamic signs.

For brand owners, the point is not that non-conventional marks are entirely new to Chinese practice, but that the revised statute now addresses them expressly. Colour, sound and dynamic signs are dealt with as signs that can function as trademarks while being subject to a specific exclusion: a sign must not be refused simply because it is unconventional, but it must not be allowed to monopolise a functional feature of the goods either.

A dynamic mark is, in essence, a mark defined by movement or change over time rather than by a static image: an animated logo, a moving sequence, or a transition that consumers recognise as identifying one undertaking. That definition drives everything else, including how the sign is filed, how distinctiveness is proved, and what the functionality exclusion is designed to keep free.

The Functionality Exclusion in Article 18

Article 18 excludes from registration signs that, for colour, sound and dynamic marks, are dictated by function rather than by brand identity. Three categories are refused:

Excluded categoryWhat it meansExample in principle
Resulting solely from the nature of the goodsThe feature is inherent in what the product isA colour or movement the product cannot avoid having
Necessary to obtain a technical effectThe feature makes the product work better or perform a functionA sound or motion that signals a mechanical operation
Giving the goods substantive valueThe feature is a major reason customers buy the productAn aesthetic effect that is itself the product's value

The distinction is between a sign that identifies the source and a feature that is the product. A distinctive animated logo may be registrable; a movement that is simply how a device operates is not. Expect examination to focus on that boundary, so prepare a description that frames the sign as a badge of origin and explains why it is not dictated by function.

How a Dynamic Mark Is Filed

The examination guidelines for dynamic marks were published in draft form and set out a specific submission package: an MP4 video of no more than 20 MB, a set of three to nine still JPEG frames, and a written description of how the mark is used. The still frames matter because the register and the public notice are static; they define what is protected when the movement cannot be reproduced in print.

Choose the frames deliberately. They should capture the recognisable states of the sequence, not simply be evenly spaced snapshots, and the written description should tie them together into a single sign rather than a collection of separate images. Inconsistency between the video, the frames and the description is a straightforward route to an objection.

Draft status, so do not treat these as final. The format requirements above come from draft examination guidelines issued for comment and may change. Confirm the current filing requirements, file formats and size limits with your agent and the official guidance in force at the time of filing, and check the official announcements and rules.

Acquired Distinctiveness and the 15-Day Evidence Window

Like any sign, a dynamic, colour or sound mark must be distinctive. Article 17 allows a sign that lacks inherent distinctiveness to become registrable where distinctiveness has been acquired through use. For non-conventional marks that question arises often: a colour or a short motion may not be inherently seen as a badge of origin, so the applicant is asked to show that consumers have come to recognise it as identifying one business.

Under the draft guidelines, where the examiner requires evidence of acquired distinctiveness, it must be submitted within 15 days of receipt of the notification. That is a short window, and the evidence is not something that can be assembled after the request arrives: it takes dated advertising, sales figures, media coverage and consumer-recognition material built up over real use.

Build the file before filing. Keep broadcast and platform records showing the animated or sound sign in use, campaign dates and reach, and examples of how the sign is presented consistently. Treat the 15-day requirement as a reason to prepare early, not as a deadline to start preparing, and remember that the draft status of the guidelines means the final period and format should be checked officially.

Building a Non-Traditional Portfolio

A non-conventional registration is a supplement to, not a replacement for, the core portfolio. File the word mark, the device mark and any Chinese-character name as separate applications first; they are simpler to clear, easier to enforce, and do not depend on a video or a sound file being reproduced correctly. Add the dynamic, colour or sound mark where the sign genuinely carries brand recognition in the market.

Then align the supporting materials: the use description, the still frames, the acquired-distinctiveness evidence and the advertising records should all describe the same sign used on the same goods. Inconsistency between the filing and the evidence is a common weakness in distinctiveness cases.

Finally, watch the implementing rules. The revised law sets the framework, but filing mechanics, formats and examination practice may be refined by revised implementing regulations and examination guidelines. Rely on the current official announcements and rules at the time you file rather than on a draft or a summary. For the underlying distinctiveness analysis see choosing a Chinese brand name, and for the separate-rights question see logo versus word mark.

Sources and Caveats

Primary sources: Articles 14, 17 and 18 of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) (adopted 26 June 2026, effective 1 January 2027; nine chapters, 87 articles); draft examination guidelines on dynamic marks covering the MP4 video of no more than 20 MB, three to nine JPEG still frames, the use description, and the 15-day period for acquired-distinctiveness evidence. The guidelines are a draft consultation text and may change. Confirm the current filing requirements and final implementing rules with CNIPA's official announcements and rules. This is general information, not legal advice.
